idiom_name: shared state-object table + context delegation (no classes needed)
implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no class hierarchy: each state is a plain (usually frozen) object literal holding the state-specific functions, the context keeps a reference and calls this.state.method(this), and a shared table of stateless states replaces per-instance state objects entirely. Classes remain an option when states share behaviour or need private fields, but plain objects plus delegation are what make the pattern nearly disappear into ordinary method calls. Keep the hand-written form when the graph is small and lives inside one module and no tooling has to reason about it.
pitfalls: Detaching a method from a state object (const { start } = states.idle) loses this; pass the context explicitly or bind the function.
Shared state objects must stay data-free - caching per-player values on states.idle makes every player share them.
The state property is writable from anywhere; route transitions through context methods so the graph cannot be bypassed.

variants.name: XState statechart actor
variants.implementation_notes: XState expresses the pattern as declarative data: createMachine declares initial, states and on transitions, createActor owns the current state and send(event) drives it, and the library supplies guards, hierarchical and parallel states, entry and exit actions, introspection and serializable snapshots. That is what the hand-written pattern lacks once the graph grows, at the cost of adopting statechart vocabulary and runtime. Use the plain-object form for a handful of states inside one object and XState when the graph is shared, visualized or persisted.
pitfalls: The actor is the state holder; keeping a second state field in your own objects creates two sources of truth.
Statechart features (guards, hierarchy, parallel regions) are heavier than the classic pattern - model only what the domain needs.
Snapshots must be restored through the library's persistence API; hand-copying actor internals breaks across versions.
